Picture a tangled riverbank. Many kinds of plants grow there. Birds sing in the bushes. Insects dart around. Worms crawl through the damp soil.

Think about this: all these different living things, each built in an intricate way, and all depending on each other, came about through natural laws still at work today.

Here's how it happens:

- Living things grow and reproduce.
- Offspring inherit traits from their parents — this comes almost automatically with reproduction.
- Traits vary because of the environment, and because of how much a creature uses or doesn't use a body part.
- Living things multiply so fast that they end up competing for limited resources. You can call this the struggle for life.
- That struggle leads to natural selection: the better-suited traits win out, species branch off in new directions, and the less successful forms die out.

So conflict, hunger, and death in nature actually produce something remarkable: the higher animals, including ourselves.

There's something grand in this way of seeing life. A handful of simple forms — maybe just one — first received the spark of life. Since then, while the planet has kept turning under the steady pull of gravity, that simple beginning has grown into countless forms. They're endlessly beautiful and wonderful. And they're still evolving right now.

- Offspring inherit traits from their parents — this comes almost automatically with reproduction.
- Traits vary, partly because of the environment and partly because of how a creature uses or fails to use its body.
- Living things multiply so fast that they must compete for limited resources. This competition is the struggle for life.

And ever since, while our planet has kept spinning through space under the steady pull of gravity, life has kept branching out from that simple start into countless beautiful and astonishing forms. That process continues today.
